opportunities.query_text: Uber burned its entire 2026 AI budget in four months, and had to cut back on usage. Agentic AI cost just doesn't behave like traditional software that we know how to budget for. I spent years at Apptio building the tooling that made cloud spend predictable, and that playbook doesn't survive contact with agents. Most teams are learning that lesson the hard way. My new piece is on why agentic AI keeps blowing out of budget, and what makes it so hard to see coming. Would like to hear from others how they are managing their AI costs.
opportunities.journalist_publication: Independent (ex-Apptio FinOps practitioner; LinkedIn/X long-form piece)
opportunities.category: AI / FinOps / Cost Management / Agentic AI
opportunities.deadline: Open (posted 2026-09-07, 'posted in last 7 days' as of this run)
opportunities.contact_method: Comment on the original X/LinkedIn post, or DM the author
opportunities.relevance_notes: The single best fit in this run and the third consecutive run it has surfaced. This is the exact problem AIToolsEssentials exists to solve: teams cannot see or predict what their AI spend is doing. Note the shift in framing since digest-2026-09-08 — the query now anchors on agentic AI cost overruns (token/consumption spend) rather than subscription overlap. AIToolsEssentials' verified-pricing dataset and keep/cut framework address the seat/subscription half of that bill, which is the half most teams can act on this week without an engineering project.
opportunities.suggested_pitch_template: Template 2 (Overlapping Subscriptions / Cost Optimization) — adapted: lead with the subscription layer of the same bill. Frame: agentic token spend is genuinely hard to forecast, but the seat-based AI subscriptions sitting next to it are auditable today. Offer the overlap data (coding x2, assistants x2, meeting notes x2) and the point that a team cutting two overlapping $20-$30 seats funds a meaningful share of the agentic budget they are worried about. Offer verified pricing snapshots with checked dates. High priority — pitch immediately, and note it has been open for several days so the window may close.

opportunities.query_text: Are you a scientist (PhD student, postdoc or beyond) paying for your own AI subscription to help with your research? I'd love to hear from you for something I'm working on at Science Magazine. Drop me a DM or reply to this thread and we can connect.
opportunities.contact_method: DM or reply to the original thread
opportunities.relevance_notes: Science Magazine is a top-tier outlet, and the query is squarely about individuals paying out of pocket for AI subscriptions — the personal-budget version of the overlap problem. It is a case-study call (they want the people, not the analyst), so the play is to supply AIToolsEssentials' aggregate data as context for the reporter rather than pitching George as the story. This is exactly the pattern where a verified pricing dataset earns a citation.
opportunities.suggested_pitch_template: Template 1 (AI Tool Pricing Changes, reactive) — adapted: offer the reporter the backdrop data for their case studies. Frame: researchers paying personally for AI subscriptions are absorbing a cost that institutions increasingly assume is covered; here is what the major plans actually cost and where they overlap (a postdoc paying for both Claude Pro and ChatGPT Plus is paying twice for one research job). Offer verified pricing snapshots with checked dates, and offer to connect them with the overlap data rather than a quote. High priority — top-tier outlet, and a citation here is worth more than a quote in a trade publication.

opportunities.query_text: Most enterprises don't have an AI strategy. They have an AI sprawl problem dressed up as one — Hundreds of agents. Dozens of models. Zero unified visibility into what they're doing, what they're consuming, or what they cost. ... The question is 'How do I safely govern hundreds of AI agents across my enterprise — without losing visibility, control, or trust?' ... I'm writing a detailed piece on this — covering AI governance architecture, agent ecosystems, model economics...
opportunities.category: Enterprise AI / Governance / Agent Sprawl / Model Economics
opportunities.deadline: Open (collecting input for upcoming article; posted 2026-09-05)
opportunities.contact_method: Comment on the LinkedIn post or DM
opportunities.relevance_notes: Carried forward from digest-2026-09-10 and still live. Directly names cost visibility ('what they're consuming, or what they cost') alongside governance. Agent sprawl is the enterprise form of the overlap problem, and AIToolsEssentials can speak to the seat-and-subscription layer that most governance frameworks skip past while going straight to token metering.
opportunities.suggested_pitch_template: Template 2 (Overlapping Subscriptions / Cost Optimization) — adapted: enterprise scale. Frame: before you can govern hundreds of agents you have to know what you already pay for — most enterprises cannot list their AI subscriptions, let alone their agents. The Stack Audit question scales: what are you paying for, is any of it redundant, what should you cut? Offer the overlap taxonomy as the inventory layer that sits underneath agent governance. High priority.

opportunities.query_text: How is AI helping employers to combat workplace fraud: expenses, product theft, time, etc? I'm looking for AI entrepreneurs/startups focused on this specific issue: the challenges and the solutions.
opportunities.journalist_publication: Independent journalist (email contact redacted on Sourcee)
opportunities.contact_method: Email (redacted on Sourcee — reply to the original #journorequest post)
opportunities.relevance_notes: Adjacent rather than core. The connection is expense visibility: shadow AI subscriptions bought on company cards are a real and under-reported line in the expense-fraud conversation, and AIToolsEssentials has the angle that the cheapest control is knowing what is already being paid for. Not a pricing story, so it ranks below the top three.
opportunities.suggested_pitch_template: Template 3 (AI Tool Directory / Comparison, general) — adapted: pitch the shadow-AI-spend angle. Frame: the fastest-growing uncontrolled line item on a company card right now is AI subscriptions bought by individual teams; before AI can police expenses it has to make existing spend visible. Offer the overlap/duplication data and the Stack Audit as the audit step. Medium priority — good fit, off the core beat.

I'm putting together a bi-weekly series called Built From Scratch, where we follow real founders and show what building a business actually looks like — not just the polished success story. ... At the end, we'll give the business a Launch Score based on things like traction, growth, product, and potential.
opportunities.category: Founders / SaaS / AI Tools / Startup Profile
opportunities.contact_method: Comment on the original post with a short description of the business
opportunities.relevance_notes: A founder-profile slot, not a pricing story — but it is an easy, low-cost brand mention and it explicitly asks for the unpolished version (what is not working), which suits an honest independent directory. Free Stack Audit is a concrete, demonstrable artifact to show a 'what's working' answer with.
opportunities.suggested_pitch_template: Template 3 (AI Tool Directory / Comparison, general) — adapted: pitch AIToolsEssentials as a bootstrapped independent tool directory that grew out of the overlap problem. Angle: 'what's completely not working' is honest material — the directory earns nothing from rankings, so the keep/cut verdicts are the product. Mention the free Stack Audit as the current traction experiment. Medium priority — brand mention, not a citation play.

summary: Three high-relevance opportunities are live and should be pitched today. The strongest is the FinOps agentic-AI-cost-overrun request (#1) — it is the core AIToolsEssentials problem, open, and has now surfaced three runs running, so the window is likely narrowing. The best outlet is Science Magazine (#2), which wants individual scientists paying out of pocket for AI subscriptions; that is a data-supply play, not a quote play, and a citation in Science is worth more than a quote in a trade publication. The enterprise agent-sprawl request (#3) stays live and directly names cost visibility. Two new medium-relevance items this run: an AI-fraud/expense request (#4) and a founder-profile series (#5). Two previously high-ranked opportunities must now be retired — the FT consulting-fee request and the Forbes tech-budgets request have both rotated off their outlet pages, which I could finally read properly this run after discovering the correct URL path (/media-outlets/<slug>/journo-requests); the earlier 'login wall' diagnosis was a wrong-URL artifact and is corrected here. Access did not improve overall: HARO is email-gated behind Cloudflare, Connectively requires login (though it is healthy — 100k+ users as of June 2026, and the stale 'platform closed' notice refers to the 2024 Cision shutdown, not the current Featured-owned service), Qwoted requires login, MentionMatch is still pre-launch, and X search is out of credits for the third consecutive run. The real fix is the newly found Medialyst MCP (medialyst.ai/api/mcp) — a free, read-only feed that normalizes Connectively, HARO, X, LinkedIn, MentionMatch and Substack with hourly polling. It needs an interactive OAuth handshake (hermes mcp add --auth oauth), which cannot be done from cron; once authorized it would replace sitemap-scraping Sourcee with a structured, authenticated feed and would likely catch requests in hours instead of days. Recommend George authorizes it. Sourcee remained the workhorse: I pulled its full 40,717-URL sitemap and date-sorted in code rather than browsing topic pages, which is both faster and more complete.
